questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Famous love stories from English literature
How to find the right partner online
What happens in our brains and bodies when we fall in love
Why people today are getting married later in life than before
questions.why: They spend the programme finding out what's going on inside our bodies and brains when we fall in love.

questions.q: According to Beth, falling in love is mostly about what?
options: Romantic words and gestures
Chemicals in the brain and body
Meeting someone at the right time
Having similar interests
questions.why: She says it's more about brain chemistry than romance – specifically hormones.

questions.q: How does Neil react to Beth's scientific explanation?
options: He jokes that she has ruined his romantic ideas
He says he already knew all about hormones from school
He disagrees and says science is wrong
He admits he has never been in love
questions.why: Neil says, “Thanks for ruining my romantic ideas, Beth!”

questions.q: What health benefit of being in love does Beth mention?
options: Better sleep and a stronger heart
Faster growth in young people and teenagers
Less need for food
Less stress and possibly a longer life
questions.why: She says being in love reduces stress and may even lengthen your life.

questions.q: What does Helen Fisher say about lust?
options: It always comes after attraction and after dopamine is released
It is caused mainly by dopamine
It often comes first, but some people don't experience it
It is the least important part of love
questions.why: She says lust often comes first, but not always, and for asexual people may not happen at all.

questions.q: According to Helen Fisher, what is the real purpose of lust?
options: To reduce stress
To help people make friends
To make romantic relationships last for the rest of our lives
To make us have children and pass on our DNA
questions.why: She says it's about the urge to mate and pass on your DNA via offspring.

questions.q: Why can strong attraction feel like an addiction?
options: Because it raises body temperature
Because dopamine makes us want to repeat it
Because testosterone makes people act without thinking
Because people stop eating and sleeping
questions.why: Fisher says dopamine gives a feel-good hit that pushes us to repeat the behaviour.

questions.q: What is Fisher implying about people who always want a new relationship?
options: They are chasing the exciting feeling that dopamine gives
They have very high levels of oestrogen and testosterone in their bodies
They are asexual and not interested in love
They are the most romantic people
questions.why: She says some people get stuck in a loop, chasing the dopamine excitement of a new relationship.
